column2: Harmonised legal requirements within scope, with provider assessment and information duties, deployer obligations and continued monitoring. Enforcement routes and timing depend on the relevant provisions.
column3: Guidance can address organisations’ actual uses and settings, including some uses outside AI Act high-risk categories. Instrument scopes differ; public transparency, named roles and legal responsibilities remain relevant.

column2: Providers retain important assessment choices, subject to substantive requirements; deployers also have context-specific duties. Some uses may fall outside high-risk classification. Internal-control, third-party and sectoral assessment routes differ. The scoped Article 111(2) transition should not be generalised to all public-sector AI.
column3: Non-statutory guidance coexists with policy and existing law. Bodies make task-specific assessment choices. Shared support and potential consequences are identified, but their sufficiency and effectiveness are not established. Specific template omissions do not erase wider duties.

column2: A public body that builds a classifier on a bought-in model may itself be the provider: the definition includes a "public authority" that "puts the AI system into service under its own name" (Art. 3(3)). Its provider and deployer responsibilities depend on the system and intended use; internal-control assessment is one applicable route, rather than unrestricted self-certification.
column3: The body makes important implementation and assessment choices within applicable legal duties, policy and guidance. The question is what evidence justifies those choices and how the justification can be scrutinised.
